name: Consent Decision-Making
use_case: A group decision procedure for when waiting for unanimous agreement drags a decision out indefinitely, or when a majority vote leaves an outvoted minority that keeps reopening or ignoring the outcome. A proposal is adopted once nobody has a reasoned objection to it, rather than once everybody actively prefers it, and each objection is treated as information that improves the proposal instead of as a veto. Best used for policies, working agreements and operational rules that can be revisited on a set review date, where an answer that is good enough for now and safe enough to try beats holding out for the perfect one.
strengths: ends open-ended debate without overruling anyone: silence is not enough, but enthusiasm is not required
every member can stop a harmful proposal, so minorities are protected without a majority being able to override them
turns disagreement into concrete amendments, because an objection has to say what harm it prevents
a built-in review date lowers the stakes and makes it easier to agree on a first version
the round structure gives quieter members the same airtime as confident ones
weaknesses: depends on a facilitator who can tell a reasoned objection from a personal preference without dismissing either
groups new to it confuse it with consensus and treat every objection as a veto, which recreates the deadlock
needs a shared, written purpose; without one there is no yardstick for testing objections
people may withhold objections to avoid conflict, so consent can be given without real agreement
unsuited to irreversible or one-shot choices where a later review cannot correct a mistake
use_cases: A school's teaching staff has spent three staff meetings on a new homework policy; waiting until every teacher is convinced has stalled it, and an earlier show of hands left half the staff disregarding the result.
A town council keeps splitting along party lines, the losing side reopens every vote at the next session, and the council wants a way of deciding that the minority can genuinely live with.
The board of a volunteer association sees outvoted members resign or stop helping after contested votes, and wants to adopt rules that nobody has a serious reason to resist.
A class or student council is setting its own rules, and the teacher wants every pupil's concerns weighed so that neither a few loud voices nor a bare majority decides for everyone.
A self-managing group with no boss to break a deadlock wants to adopt a new rule quickly and revise it after a trial period, instead of arguing until every member is enthusiastic.
